A spike in the bond yields of CoreWeave, a cloud provider that rents out AI computing power, revived worries about debt-heavy AI customers and dragged semiconductor shares lower, according to Yahoo Finance. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), both an investor in CoreWeave and its chip supplier, slipped with the group. Nvidia designs the processors and networking gear that train and run AI models, and sells them as complete data center systems to cloud giants, AI labs, and specialists like CoreWeave. Gamers know it for its graphics cards, but data centers now bring in the vast majority of its revenue. So the selloff raised a sharp question: is Nvidia's growth only as sturdy as the balance sheets of the companies buying its chips? The answer depends less on one cloud provider than on who else is paying. Whatever its customers are doing, Nvidia itself is enormously profitable. Over the past 12 months, it earned $192.88 billion in net income and kept about 65% of its sales as operating profit. Those margins come from pricing power: buyers pay up because Nvidia sells the chips, the networking, and the software developers already build on. That edge has compounded for years, with revenue growing about 66.9% a year over the past five years. AI spending has been the common thread for the wider chip group covered in 12 Best Performing Semiconductor Stocks to Invest In. The latest results show the moat widening. In its fiscal second quarter of 2027, revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, and data center revenue rose 117% to $89.0 billion. Management guided third-quarter revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, without counting on any data center compute sales in China. The customer list argues against a single point of failure. The new Vera Rubin platform is in full production at partners including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle, not just CoreWeave, and CEO Jensen Huang said in the release that a broader base of AI labs and startups is scaling at the same time. Nvidia is also lining up outside money: financing platforms with firms including Apollo, BlackRock, and KKR aim to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital, subject to final agreements. The buildout behind those orders runs well beyond chips, into the names in 15 Best Data Center Stocks to Buy and Hold for the Next Decade. That financing push cuts both ways, and it's the heart of the bear case. Specialist providers like CoreWeave are building AI capacity with borrowed money, and Nvidia sits on both sides of some of those deals, as supplier and investor. This week, CoreWeave's debt load and the prospect of higher interest rates were enough to shake the whole chip group, according to Yahoo Finance. Huang pushed back at a Bloomberg event in Stockholm, saying CoreWeave's position is strengthening and its cost of capital is falling, according to Yahoo Finance. Still, a credit squeeze would hit the most leveraged buyers first, and it would show up as softer orders long before it touched Nvidia's margins. For now, the guidance points the other way. The market has marked the stock down for exactly this risk. Nvidia trades at about 23 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, roughly 45% below its five-year average of about 42 times, and only modestly above the technology sector's median of about 21 times. That small premium is the striking part, given that analysts' consensus expects earnings per share to grow about 95% this fiscal year. The five-year average was set when investors paid ahead for growth that hadn't arrived; now the earnings have arrived, and the multiple has fallen to meet them. Investors hunting for AI exposure at a lower price have a wider set to weigh in 10 Undervalued AI Stocks to Buy Now. The multiple rests on adjusted earnings, which came in below GAAP earnings last quarter, so it isn't flattering the picture. What the price does assume is that growth slows sharply after this year, or that the financing chain behind AI spending breaks. The evidence points to a valuation reflecting financing fears more than any crack in the business. For investors who can sit through sharp swings in chip stocks and are looking several years out, the setup looks stronger than the selloff suggests. A guidance cut tied to customers pulling back on borrowed spending, or financing platforms that fail to reach final agreements, would change that picture quickly. title: Martin Shkreli Says New Photonic Chips Could Run Circles Around Nvidia - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Martin Shkreli just named three private startups he believes could threaten Nvidia's dominance in AI chips, and his reasoning involves a technology that computes at the speed of light. The catch is that Nvidia may already be one step ahead. Martin Shkreli thinks the next serious challenge to NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) could run on light. On an All-In podcast episode released October 12, 2026, the former hedge fund manager named three private startups building optical chips and said their designs “would run circles around what Nvidia does.” The comment comes during a rough stretch for the stock. Nvidia shares fell 6.39% over the past week as chip stocks slid in a global tech rout on AI funding worries. Shkreli told the hosts he is exploring the field himself. “So we’re investigating, maybe we’ll start a company or something like that. But there are a couple of startups like Neurofos, Opticore, Lumi that want to make these photonic matmul cores which would run circles around what Nvidia does. Now of course that’s not the whole story. There are a lot of details and nonlinearity and storage.” He said the optical calculations “happen in instant time.” Neurofos, Opticore and Lumi are private, so public investors have no direct way to own them and no disclosed financials to evaluate. AI models mostly run on matrix multiplication (“matmul”): multiplying enormous grids of numbers over and over. A GPU does that math by pushing electrons through billions of transistors, which burns power and throws off heat. A photonic chip encodes numbers in beams of light and lets them interact as they pass through optical components, so the answer comes out as the light crosses the chip. That gives you the speed and energy appeal. Shkreli’s cautions carry real weight. Neural networks also need nonlinear steps between multiplications (functions that decide which signals pass forward), and light handles those poorly. Models also need memory to hold their weights and data, and that storage remains electronic. Any photonic core still needs conventional silicon wrapped around it. Any competition faces a company at full speed. title: Cathie Wood-Led Ark Invest's Biggest Q3 Winners and Losers — PLTR, NVDA, TXG Led While TSLA, RKLB Dragged - Stocktwits
content: Cathie Wood-led Ark Invest's portfolios saw some dramatic winners and losers in the third quarter (Q3), with artificial intelligence, biotech, crypto and other disruptive-technology bets among the biggest drivers. Ark's latest quarterly report shows that several stocks made meaningful contributions across multiple ETFs, while Tesla Inc. (TSLA) and Rocket Lab Corp. (RKLB) emerged among the most notable drags. Ark's attribution figures measure each holding's contribution to its ETF's performance, rather than the stock's standalone return. 10x Genomics Inc. (TXG) was the standout winner across Ark's portfolios. The stock contributed 9.03 percentage points to ARK Genomic Revolution ETF’s (ARKG) 28.92% Q3 gain and 2.92 points to ARK Innovation ETF’s (ARKK) 10.39% return during the quarter. Ark attributed the rally to growing interest in single-cell sequencing and spatial analysis as sources of data for AI drug-discovery models. The firm also highlighted the launch of 10x's Atera spatial system, with orders already in place for the 40 shipments anticipated in 2026. Twist Bioscience Corp. (TWST) was another major biotech winner, contributing 6.51 points to ARKG and 2.55 points to ARKK. The stock jumped 87.83% during the quarter. Ark said Twist was increasingly recognized as a beneficiary of AI-driven drug discovery, including through its protein-characterization work for Anthropic. Tempus AI Inc. (TEM) also stood out, contributing 3.21 points to ARKG and 2.08 points to ARKK, while gaining 41.38% during the quarter. Then there was Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR), emerging as one of the most important cross-ETF winners. Palantir contributed 1.86 points to ARK Autonomous Technology & Robotics ETF (ARKQ), 1.62 points to ARKK, 1.48 points to ARK Next Generation Technology ETF (ARKW), 2.39 points to ARK Blockchain & Fintech Innovation ETF (ARKF) and 1.47 points to ARK Space & Defense Innovation ETF (ARKX). Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) also made the cut, particularly across Ark's technology-focused portfolios. It contributed 0.49 points to ARKQ and 0.48 points to ARKX. Tesla was the clearest recurring drag across Ark's portfolios. It was the biggest detractor in ARKQ (-1.72 percentage points), ARKK (-1.75 points) and ARKW (-1.43 points). Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. The waiver, issued Friday, comes less than a month after Trump signed the Graham Act into law and about a week after the administration’s diesel deal with Russia. The Graham Act, signed into law on Sept. 18, authorized sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia and certain foreign persons and countries. The law also allows the president to waive those measures if he certifies to Congress that doing so is in the national interest of the U.S. Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order invokes that authority, stating that he has submitted the required certification and report to Congress. The president waived the application of duties provided under key sections of the Graham Act, as well as several sanctions and restrictions targeting foreign persons. However, the order leaves a framework in place for potentially steep tariffs on Russian goods and countries that continue to buy Russian energy or facilitate sanctions evasion. The waiver will remain in effect until Trump or the Secretary of State, in consultation with other senior officials, determines that further action is appropriate. Existing Russia-related sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders have been kept in place. Trump’s executive order also laid out a sweeping tariff structure that could be activated against Russia and countries involved in Russian energy trade. The order calls for a 500% ad valorem duty on goods from Russia, subject to exceptions in the Graham Act and the waivers issued by Trump. It also provides for an additional 100% tariff on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas if those countries knowingly make new purchases of Russian-origin crude or natural gas on or after Oct. 18. The order directs the U.S. Trade Representative, working with the State, Treasury and Energy departments, to monitor Russian oil and gas purchases and sanctions evasion and regularly report developments to Trump. U.S. government bond prices retreated, and the dollar suffered its sharpest weekly decline in over a month during the week ending Oct. 16, as fixed-income investors digested ambiguous signals from Kevin Warsh on the future course of interest rates. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to provide forward guidance on interest rate trajectory during remarks at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok. Warsh's silence led traders to pare back probabilities of an October rate hike to 20%. "Warsh offered no guidance, which while it should be expected of him at this point, the market is taking it as a signal that the October Fed meeting is likely a no go," Noah Buffam at CIVB Capital Markets told Bloomberg in an interview. Moreover, adding to the dissent among fixed income traders, the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not provide information or explicit proposals to reduce long-duration debt issuances or eliminate 20-year auctions, which primary dealers were expecting. The 30-year U.S. Treasury yield slipped 17 basis points from the previous week to 5.43%, while the 10-year yield eased slightly to 5.08% and 2-year yields settled at 4.72% for the week ending Oct. 16. The spread between the U.S. 10-year yield and the U.S. 2-year yield ticked lower to 0.37% in the week, from 0.44% a week ago. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury ETF (TLT) ended the week 2.7% higher, while the shorter-duration iShares 1-3 year ETF (SHY) added about 0.2%. The slight recovery in the shorter-duration bond ETF may reflect easing short-term inflation pressure; however, markets still factor in one more rate hike in December. Retail sentiment on TLT and SHY was ‘bullish,’ with ‘high’ message volumes. Yield curve flattening trends persisted as short-duration yields outpaced gains at the long end, keeping the gap between 2-year and 10-year Treasuries tightly compressed. The bond rout expanded across international sovereign bond markets. European government bond yields rose alongside U.S. peers, with German Bunds, UK Gilts and French bonds all remaining elevated amid soaring inflation pressures. The Dollar Spot Index slipped 0.2% on Friday, snapping a multi-week rally and registering its worst weekly performance since September 4. The dollar fell against all major developed market currencies, allowing the euro to break a five-week losing streak. Hotter-than-expected September CPI data and solid retail sales initially supported rate-hike expectations earlier in the week, but investors questioned the durability of the artificial intelligence boom that has supported U.S. growth, putting pressure on the greenback. content: OpenAI changed the world four years ago when it launched its artificial intelligence (AI) model, ChatGPT, sparking an AI revolution that led to the emergence of multiple competing models. It recently postponed its plans to go public, which means investors don't have access to its financial data beyond what it chooses to disclose. Since it's not a public company, its growth rates aren't directly relevant to investors, but many still track them to gauge the pace of AI development more broadly. For example, if companies like OpenAI and rival Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI model, are growing rapidly, they'll likely need more data center processing power. That would be great news for Nvidia (NVDA -1.43%), which supplies a large fraction of the processors that power data centers. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images. Conversely, if it looks like demand for AI accelerator chips is waning, the market sours on Nvidia, and that's what happened last week. OpenAI said it had a $50 billion revenue run rate, $18 billion less than the figure that was previously circulating. Several AI stocks tanked on the news, including Nvidia, which is down 4% since the news came out. That might not sound like a lot, but for a $5 trillion company, it translates into $200 billion. Should retail investors view this as a buying opportunity? Nvidia isn't the only AI chipmaker around, but its chips are critical providers of power for the high-level inference and reasoning that support AI functions. That means all large models require Nvidia chips and, increasingly, full Nvidia compute systems. It recently launched its latest platform, Vera Rubin, which combines Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs), Vera central processing units (CPUs), large quantities of high bandwidth memory, and other hardware to deliver high processing power. The company's revenue growth has recently accelerated, with the top line more than doubling year over year in its fiscal 2027 second quarter (which ended July 26). Management already provided fiscal 2028 guidance for 70% growth, which would be a serious feat given how large the company already is. That 4% drop doesn't on its own create an incredible buying opportunity. However, it might be a good time to buy the stock if you've been planning to anyway. The more pressing concern is what the market is actually worried about: whether OpenAI's news is actually bad news for Nvidia. There's some risk there that investors should keep in mind. Automaker and chip supplier partnerships in automated driving have become a recurring template in the sector, and expansions of existing tie-ups tend to matter less for the carmaker's near-term earnings than as signals about platform commitment. The pattern in comparable episodes is that the semiconductor partner captures the more visible re-rating, since design wins of this kind feed directly into automotive revenue pipelines, while for the OEM the announcement is largely a validation of its software and autonomy roadmap rather than a measurable financial event. The distinction worth drawing is between announcements that specify the depth of integration, such as named platforms, vehicle generations, or production timelines, and those that restate intent; the former have historically carried more weight with the peer set and with sell-side estimates. Mercedes has prior form in this space, having run technology collaborations on driving assistance systems for some time, so an expansion is continuation rather than a strategic pivot. What is worth watching next is any accompanying detail on scope, such as which vehicle programmes are covered and whether other suppliers are displaced, plus whether rival OEMs respond with parallel announcements, since clustering of such deals has tended to mark phases of the autonomy investment cycle. title: Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA Expand Strategic Partnership to Advance Safe Highly Automated Driving in the Next Decade - NVIDIA Newsroom
content:
Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA today announced that they will extend their strategic partnership to advance the next generation of automated driving systems. The collaboration brings together Mercedes-Benz’s automotive engineering and safety expertise and its MB.OS operating system with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI technologies. “NVIDIA is our most important strategic partner in automated driving. Together, we developed the first Mercedes-Benz assistance system for urban point-to-point driving for the western world,” Jörg Burzer, member of the board of management of Mercedes‑Benz Group AG and chief technology officer, development and procurement. “The expansion of our partnership marks a significant milestone and reflects the mutual trust we have built over the years. Together, we aim to bring further pioneering innovations to the road, offering our customers the best automated driving experience while upholding the high safety standards they expect from a Mercedes-Benz.” “Accelerated computing is giving vehicles the intelligence to understand the world and reason through complex driving situations,” said Ali Kani, vice president of automotive at NVIDIA. “Mercedes-Benz brings the engineering excellence and commitment to safety this transformation demands. Together, we’re building on NVIDIA Hyperion to bring that intelligence and full-stack safety to the road and make autonomous driving an everyday reality.” Mercedes-Benz’s MB.OS operating system supports new driving functions and over-the-air updates, working with NVIDIA Hyperion’s in-vehicle computing and sensor architecture. NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack provides full-stack driving software with AI reasoning capabilities, supporting point-to-point urban assistance, active safety and automated parking. NVIDIA Halos adds to the Mercedes-Benz safety foundation, including a parallel safety stack that adds redundancy and guardrails. Together, these technologies support advanced driver assistance and the development of future SAE-Level 4 applications, including robolimousines. Beyond automated driving, Mercedes-Benz also relies on NVIDIA technologies for vehicle engineering simulation and within MO360, its digital production ecosystem — from virtual planning to AI-based applications. Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang addressed the recent discord at key partner and fallen AI stock darling CoreWeave (CRWV) on Thursday, expressing optimism in the data center operator following a 15% rout on Wednesday and a smaller dip on Thursday morning. CoreWeave stock fell again on Friday during premarket trading, with the AI company's shares slipping 4%. "CoreWeave's strength is improving every day," Huang shared at a Bloomberg event in Stockholm. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing." His input was much anticipated this week as concerns about the health of CoreWeave and its exposures to Nvidia have continued to build. Huang's need to weigh in wasn't a surprise to veteran tech analyst Tal Liani, who just this morning published a bullish note on CoreWeave with an aggressive $140 price target. "Don't forget that Nvidia is basically financing all these deals with them, with other hyperscalers because they want to block off the competition. They want to make sure that CoreWeave and others are using Nvidia GPUs and not AMD GPUs," Liani said on Sozzi Unleashed. Liani added, "So at the end of the day, there is an inherent interest both ways. And I'm sure that you're going to hear from everyone on the planet that has a vested interest in the build-out of data centers. You're going to hear comforting kinds of comments about the validity of the demand and the sustainability of the demand, including Jensen. It's just a question of time." CoreWeave's corporate bonds across maturities have continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet. The selling spread to other AI cloud stocks: Nebius (NBIS) fell 11%, Oracle (ORCL) dropped another 9%, and the following stocks sank more than 10%: DigitalOcean (DOCN), Hut 8 (HUT), Cipher (CIFR), TeraWulf (WULF), and IREN (IREN). title: History Says Nvidia Stock Usually Rises in the Fourth Quarter -- It Has in 20 of the Last 27 - The Motley Fool
content: Two of the seven down years erased over half the stock's value. What went wrong? Shares of Nvidia (NVDA -1.43%) hit another record on Tuesday, Oct. 6, closing at $239.24. If history's any guide, the October-to-December quarter has usually been a good one for the artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant's stock. Measured from the end of September to the end of December, Nvidia's shares rose in 20 of the 27 years from 1999 through 2025. The median change for all 27 fourth quarters was a gain of around 14%. But the record comes with two caveats. Nvidia's stock has climbed in most quarters during this stretch, not just the last one of the year. From 2000 through 2025, for example, it also gained in 20 of 26 first quarters. And two of the seven fourth quarters that went wrong cost shareholders over half their money. I think the calendar matters much less here than the report Nvidia puts out in the middle of it. Nvidia's fiscal year ends in late January, so its fiscal third quarter closes in late October. The report for that period tends to come in mid-to-late November, about halfway through the calendar fourth quarter. That report also gives management's revenue outlook for the fiscal fourth quarter, which runs roughly from November through January. Sure, even a great report doesn't promise a good quarter. Nvidia's fiscal third-quarter 2026 results, released Nov. 19, 2025, showed revenue up 62% year over year to $57.0 billion. Management also guided for $65.0 billion in the next quarter. The stock dropped around 3% a day later. It closed the fourth quarter down 0.04% -- a paper-thin loss in a quarter when the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -2.15%) gained around 3%. Nvidia's two worst fourth quarters broke the pattern for very different reasons. In 2000, the stock lost 60% as the dot-com crash pulled down tech stocks broadly. The Nasdaq Composite slid by around a third during the same three months. But Nvidia's shares were back above their late-September 2000 price by April 2001. The 2018 decline was mainly Nvidia's own problem, and the November report made it far worse. By report day, shares had already fallen about 28% from their late-September close. For the three months ended Oct. 28, 2018 (Nvidia's fiscal third quarter of 2019), revenue grew 21% year over year to $3.18 billion. But management forecast fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $2.70 billion, around 15% below what the company had just reported. "Our near-term results reflect excess channel inventory post the cryptocurrency boom, which will be corrected," CEO Jensen Huang said in the earnings release. Put simply, too many of Nvidia's chips sat unsold with distributors and retailers after demand from cryptocurrency miners cooled. Shares fell about 19% the day after the report and ended the quarter down 52%, versus a loss of about 18% for the Nasdaq. They didn't climb back above their late-September 2018 close till February 2020. Notably, most of Nvidia's down fourth quarters lined up with a falling market. The Nasdaq fell in five of the seven. Only in 2020 and last year did Nvidia's shares drop while the index gained. Nvidia's business now looks nothing like it did in late 2018. For its fiscal second quarter of 2027 (which ended on July 26, 2026), revenue more than doubled, climbing 106% year over year to $96.2 billion. Management's forecast calls for $108.0 billion in fiscal Q3, plus or minus 2%. That's the bar the fiscal third-quarter report needs to clear. Meeting the guide would mean growth of about 89% from the $57.0 billion Nvidia reported a year earlier, a step down from 106%. The forecast for the following quarter could matter even more to the stock than the quarter itself. Nvidia's shares sell for around 15 times the consensus earnings estimate for fiscal 2028 (the year ending January 2028). Broadcom, another AI chipmaker, costs about 19 times its consensus earnings estimate for its next fiscal year. True, a price-to-earnings ratio is only as good as the estimates behind it. But at that price, Nvidia's shares could arguably weather a weaker report than the past few. So, does the calendar make Nvidia stock a buy right now? Not on its own. Twenty up years out of 27 mainly reflect a stock that's climbed in most quarters, whatever the season. And the worst years that broke the pattern saw a falling market, a weak forecast from Nvidia, or both. At today's price, I'd consider buying shares for the growth Nvidia is delivering. The fourth quarter's history doesn't do much for that case. Daniel Sparks and his clients do not have positions in any of the stocks mentioned.
